items.new: In considering these ribs, I could not help being struck anew with the point so often repeated in this book: that the skeleton of the whale is by no means the mold of his living form. The largest of the Tranque ribs, one of the middle ones, occupied that part of the fish which, in life, is greatest in depth. Now, the greatest depth of the living body of this particular whale must have been at least sixteen feet, whereas the corresponding rib measured only a little more than eight feet. So that this rib conveyed only half the true sense of the living magnitude of that part. Besides, for some distance along where I now saw only a naked spine, everything had once been wrapped round with tons of added bulk in flesh, muscle, blood, and bowels. Still more: for the ample fins, I saw only a few disordered joints; and in place of the weighty and majestic but boneless flukes, an utter blank!

items.new: But by far the most wonderful of all cetacean relics was the almost complete vast skeleton of an extinct monster, found in 1842 on the plantation of Judge Creagh in Alabama. The awestruck, credulous slaves in the vicinity took it for the bones of one of the fallen angels. The Alabama doctors declared it a huge reptile and bestowed upon it the name of Basilosaurus. But some specimen bones of it being taken across the sea to Owen, the English anatomist, it turned out that this alleged reptile was a whale, though of a vanished species. A significant illustration of the fact, again and again repeated in this book, that the skeleton of the whale gives only a little clue to the shape of his fully living body. So Owen rechristened the monster Zeuglodon; and in his paper read before the London Geological Society, pronounced it, in substance, one of the most extraordinary creatures which the changes of the globe have wiped from existence.

items.new: When I stand among these mighty Leviathan skeletons, skulls, tusks, jaws, ribs, and vertebrae — all showing partial resemblances to the existing breeds of sea-monsters, but at the same time bearing similar likenesses to the annihilated Leviathans from before recorded time, their incalculable elders — I am carried back as if by a flood to that wondrous period before time itself can be said to have begun; for time began with man. Here Saturn's gray chaos rolls over me, and I catch dim, shuddering glimpses of those polar eternities when wedged bastions of ice pressed hard on what are now the Tropics, and in all the 25,000 miles of this world's circumference not a hand's breadth of habitable land was visible. Then the whole world was the whale's; and, king of creation, he left his wake along the present lines of the Andes and the Himalayas. Who can show a pedigree like Leviathan? Ahab's harpoon had shed older blood than Pharaoh's. Methuselah seems a schoolboy. I look around to shake hands with Shem. I am horror-struck at the unspeakable terrors of the whale, whose existence is older than Moses and has no source, and which, having been before all time, must surely go on existing after all human ages are over.

And if I ever go where Pliny is, I, a whaleman (more of one than he was), will make bold to tell him so. items.new: Nor, rightly considered, does it seem to be any argument for the gradual extinction of the sperm whale, for example, that in former years (the latter part of the last century, say) these Leviathans were met in small pods much more often than at present, and that as a result the voyages were not so long and were also much more profitable. Because, as has been noted elsewhere, those whales, influenced by some considerations of safety, now swim the seas in immense caravans, so that to a large degree the scattered solitaries, yokes, pods, and schools of other days are now gathered into vast but widely separated, infrequent armies. That is all. And equally mistaken seems the idea that because the so-called whale-bone whales no longer haunt many grounds that once abounded with them, that species too must be declining. For they are only being driven from promontory to cape; and if one coast is no longer enlivened with their spouts, then, you may be sure, some other and remoter shore has very recently been startled by the unfamiliar spectacle.

items.new: Nor, at the time, had it failed to enter his monomaniac mind that all the anguish of that present suffering was nothing but the direct result of an earlier woe. And he seemed to see all too plainly that just as the most poisonous reptile of the marsh perpetuates its kind as inevitably as the sweetest songbird of the grove, so, equally with every happiness, all miserable events naturally beget their like. Yes, more than equally, thought Ahab, since both the ancestry and the descendants of Grief reach further than the ancestry and descendants of Joy. For, leaving aside this point — that it is an inference from certain church teachings that while some natural pleasures here will have no children born to them in the other world, but, on the contrary, will be followed by the joy-childlessness of all hell's despair, some guilty mortal miseries will still fruitfully beget for themselves an eternally growing brood of griefs beyond the grave — leaving that aside entirely, there still seems to be an inequality in the deeper analysis of the thing. For, thought Ahab, while even the highest earthly happiness always has a certain meaningless pettiness lurking in it, all heart-woes have at bottom a mystic significance, and in some men an archangelic grandeur; and careful tracing-out of them does not contradict the obvious conclusion. To trace the family trees of these high mortal miseries leads us at last among the sourceless first-born lines of the gods; so that, in the face of all the glad, haymaking suns and the soft, cymbal-clashing round harvest moons, we must give in to this: that the gods themselves are not forever glad. The ineradicable, sad birthmark on the brow of man is only the stamp of sorrow in those who signed it.

items.new: Unwittingly here a secret has been divulged which perhaps might more properly have been disclosed before, in due order. Along with many other particulars concerning Ahab, it had always remained a mystery to some why, for a certain period both before and after the sailing of the Pequod, he had hidden himself away with such grand-lama-like seclusion, and for that one interval sought speechless refuge, as it were, among the marble senate of the dead. Captain Peleg's rumored reason for this seemed by no means adequate, though indeed, where all Ahab's deeper nature was concerned, every revelation partook more of significant darkness than of explanatory light. But in the end it all came out — this one matter did, at least. That dreadful mishap was at the bottom of his temporary seclusion. And not only this, but to that ever-shrinking, dwindling circle ashore who, for any reason, possessed the privilege of a less prohibited approach to him — to that timid circle the above-hinted accident, remaining as it did moodily unexplained by Ahab, invested itself with terrors not entirely unrelated to the land of spirits and of wails. So that, through their concern for him, they had all conspired, so far as they could, to hush up the knowledge of this thing from others. And hence it was that not till a considerable time had passed did it come to light upon the Pequod's decks.
